doc.title: Bob Rosengarden interviewed by Monk Rowe, Clinton, New York, October 6, 1996

title: Brazilian music versus Latin rhythm
summary: He explains his love of Brazilian music, Jobim and Bonfa, and how it differs from Latin feel.

story.theme_name: Playing with Coltrane and the avant-garde

blocks.x: It’s true. It’s called music. I listen at home, to my wife’s chagrin, I listen to long hair music almost all the time. The only other kind of music I listen to is Brazilian music. I have a soft spot in my head for that. And I got friendly with a lot of the Brazilians — Jobim and Luiz Bonfa. I saw Black Orpheus 37 times, you know, and I said oh my God, what is that, and loved it, and became, I was the only gringo who could imitate that.
Right. And knew the difference between the different Latin styles. I mean it’s one thing to say well play this Latin. Well there’s a lot of —

Well Brazilian is different from Latin. I mean Latin’s over here and Brazilian’s over here. It’s closer akin to jazz, the feeling of, it’s in a technical sense, Latin music is generally in even eights [scats]. And Brazilian is [scats]. You know kids in school I tell them see this? It’s not this, it’s [scats]. And you have to imitate it with your mouth, the sound [scats]. Listen to the Portuguese language, you know, it’s very musical. It undulates.
I love that vocalization. It’s what Clark does too. You know if he’s trying to get a point out to some students —
